Keep going in order: try 3, then 4, then 5, and so on. We get 3 times 28 and 4 times 21.
Carry on the same way: 6 times 14 and 7 times 12. 5 does not divide 84, so we skip it.
When do we stop? The next factor after 7 is 12, and 12 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 6 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 6 pairs. So we double 6.

beats.say: 6 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 12. So 84 has 12 factors. Here they all are, in order.
So to count factors: write the pairs in order, stop when they start to repeat, and count 2 for each pair. Your turn next!
Three of these numbers can be made by adding two primes. One cannot. We test each one.
5 is 2 plus 3. 7 is 2 plus 5. Remember, 2 is a prime number. So both of those can be made.
12 is 5 plus 7, and both are prime. So 12 can be made too.
Now 11. It is odd. Two odd primes add up to an even number, so to make 11, one of the primes has to be 2, the only even prime.
11 minus 2 is 9. Is 9 a prime number?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 3 is 9. So 9 has a factor other than 1 and itself, and it is not prime.

beats.say: 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime. There is no other way to try. So 11 is not the sum of two primes.
The trap: 11 is a prime number itself. But that does not mean it can be split into two primes.
Ajay rolls three dice. The three numbers multiply to make 90. What do they add up to? Remember, a die only shows 1 to 6.
Break 90 into its prime factors: 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
Look at the 5. Could it join with another prime on one die? 5 times 2 is 10, and 5 times 3 is 15.

ask.ifNot: A die only goes up to 6. 10 and 15 are both too big, so the 5 must sit on a die by itself.

beats.say: So one die shows 5. The other two dice must multiply to make 90 divided by 5, which is 18.
How can two dice make 18? 2 times 9 would need a 9, and a die has no 9. So it must be 3 times 6.
The dice show 3, 5 and 6. Check: 3 times 5 times 6 is 90.
Add them up. 3 plus 5 plus 6 is 14.
Only one set of dice fits, so we do have enough information. The key was that a die stops at 6.
What is the smallest number we can add to 267 times 348, so that 5 divides the total? Good news: we do not need the whole product.
A number is divisible by 5 only when it ends in 0 or 5. So all that matters is the last digit of the product.
The last digit of a product comes from the two ones digits. Here they are 7 and 8, and 7 times 8 is 56. So what digit does the product end in?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56, and 56 ends in 6. So the whole product ends in 6.

beats.say: The product ends in 6. Counting on from 6, the next ending that 5 likes is 0. And 6 needs 4 more to reach 10.
So the smallest number to add is 4.
Let's check with the full product. 267 times 348 is 92,916. Add 4, and we get 92,920. It ends in 0, so 5 divides it.
The trap is adding 5. That would make the number end in 1. For the 5 test, only the last digit matters.
Find the L C M of 48 and 54. L C M means lowest common multiple: the first number that both 48 and 54 reach when you count up in their tables.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 54?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 54 is 54 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 54, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: The simplest way is to count up in both tables until they meet. Count up in 48s: 48, 96, 144, 192, 240, 288, 336, 384, 432.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 48 and 54?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 432 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 432 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 432.
Let's check. 432 divided by 48 is 9, and 432 divided by 54 is 8. Both divide exactly, so 432 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 48 by 54 gives 2592. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 432 gets there first.
So for an L C M: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the answer. Your turn next!
Two ribbons, 84 metres and 108 metres long. Both are cut into pieces of the same length, with nothing left over. How long can each piece be?

board.text: Ribbons: 84 m and 108 m. Equal pieces, none left.

spec.note: Equal pieces, as long as possible.

beats.say: The piece length must divide 84 exactly, and 108 exactly. We want the greatest such length. What is that?

ask.ifNot: A length that divides both ribbons exactly is a common factor. The greatest one is the highest common factor.

beats.say: So we want the H C F. Here are the factors of 84. We will test them on 108, starting from the big end.
84, 42, 28, 21 and 14 do not divide 108. It is not in any of their tables. Cross them out.
Next is 12. Does 12 divide 108 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 9 is 108. So 12 divides 108 exactly.

beats.say: 12 times 9 is 108, and 12 times 7 is 84. So each piece can be 12 metres long: 7 pieces from one ribbon, and 9 from the other.
Watch the traps. 6 divides both ribbons, but it is not the greatest. And 14 divides only 84, so the longer ribbon would have some left over.
How many factors does 30 have? A factor of 30 is a number that divides 30 exactly, with nothing left over.
Here is a neat trick. Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 30. The first pair is easy: 1 times 30.
Next we try 2. 30 is even, so 2 is a factor. What is its partner?

ask.ifNot: The partner is the number we multiply 2 by to make 30. Half of 30 is 15, so the partner of 2 is 15.

beats.say: 2 times 15 is 30. That is our second pair.
Keep going in order: try 3, then 4, then 5, and so on. We get 3 times 10 and 5 times 6. 4 does not divide 30, so we skip it.
When do we stop? The next factor after 5 is 6, and 6 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 4 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 4 pairs. So we double 4.

beats.say: 4 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 8. So 30 has 8 factors. Here they all are, in order.
Remember the plan: go up in order, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and write each pair that works. Then count the numbers in the pairs.
A four-digit number: 8, star, 2, star. Both stars are the same digit, and 9 divides the number exactly. Which digit is the star?

spec.note: Both stars are the same digit.

beats.say: The test for 9: add up all the digits. If the total is in the 9 times table, then 9 divides the number.
The digits we know are 8 and 2. They add up to 10.
The two stars are the same digit. So together they add up to double that digit, and a double is always an even number.
The total must land in the 9 times table: 18 or 27. For that, the stars must add 8 or 17. Which of those can two equal digits make?

ask.ifNot: Two equal digits always add up to an even number. 17 is odd, so it must be 8.

beats.say: The two stars add up to 8, and half of 8 is 4. So each star is 4.
Let's check. The digits add up to 18, which is in the 9 times table. And the number is 8,424, which is 9 times 936.
One trap: 8 is what the two stars add up to together. It is not one star. Share it equally between the two.
We need the sum of the L C M and the H C F of 24 and 32. That is three jobs: find the H C F, find the L C M, then add them.
Start by breaking each number into prime factors, the building blocks it is made of.
Take 24. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 3 is left. So 24 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3.
Take 32. It is made only of 2s: 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
First the H C F. It is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 24 and 32 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Both lines have three 2s. 2 times 2 times 2 is 8, so the H C F is 8.
Now the L C M. It must hold all of 24 and all of 32. So we take each prime the most times it shows up in one number: five 2s and one 3. Multiply them, and we get 96.
A quick check on the L C M. 96 divided by 24 is 4, and 96 divided by 32 is 3. Both are exact.
We have the H C F, 8, and the L C M, 96. Now the last job. What do we work out to finish?

ask.ifNot: Sum means add. And it is the L C M and the H C F that we add, not the two numbers we started with.

beats.say: 96 plus 8 is 104. That is our answer.
Read the question with care: sum means add, difference means subtract. And do finish the last step. The L C M on its own is not the answer.
Write down every prime number between 1 and 100. How many times is the digit 2 used? We need the primes that have a 2 in them.

board.text: Primes from 1 to 100: how many times is 2 used?

beats.say: A 2 can sit in the ones place or in the tens place. Take the ones place first. Any number that ends in 2 is even.
Which is the only prime number that ends in 2?

ask.ifNot: 12 and 22 are even, so 2 divides them and they are not prime. The only even prime is 2 itself.

beats.say: So the ones place gives us one 2: the prime number 2.
Now the tens place: the numbers from 20 to 29. The even ones are not prime. That leaves the odd ones: 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29.
Careful here. 21 is 3 times 7. 25 is 5 times 5. 27 is 3 times 9. None of those is prime.
23 and 29 are prime, and each has one 2. So the primes with a 2 are 2, 23 and 29. That is 3 times.
The trap is counting numbers like 12 and 22. They have a 2 in them, but they are not prime. And do not forget the prime 2 itself.
Use every one-digit prime number, once each, to make the greatest odd number.

board.text: Use all the one-digit primes. Greatest odd number = ?

beats.say: First, which are the one-digit primes?

ask.ifNot: 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime. 1 is not prime either. And do not forget 2, the only even prime.

beats.say: So our digits are 2, 3, 5 and 7.
For the greatest number, we put the biggest digits first. That would give 7532. But look at the end: it finishes in 2, so it is even.
The number must be odd. Keep 7 and 5 at the front. Which digit must go last: 3 or 2?

ask.ifNot: An odd number must end in an odd digit. 2 is even, so the 3 goes last.

beats.say: So 7, then 5, then 2, and 3 at the end. The greatest odd number is 7523.
Two traps. 9 is not prime, so it cannot be used. And 7325 is odd too, but it is smaller, because 5 hundreds beats 3 hundreds.
Look at 73251. Two of its digits change places, and then 6 must divide the new number exactly. Which two digits?
6 is 2 times 3. So a number that 6 divides must pass two tests: the test for 2, and the test for 3.
Test for 3: add the digits. 7 plus 3 plus 2 plus 5 plus 1 is 18, and 18 is in the 3 times table. Swapping digits never changes the sum, so this test is always passed.
Test for 2: the number must be even. So what kind of digit must be at the end?

ask.ifNot: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. So the last digit has to be even.

beats.say: Look at the digits: 7, 3, 2, 5, 1. Only one of them is even: the 2. So the 2 must move to the end, where the 1 is now.
Swap the 2 and the 1, and we get 73152. It ends in 2, so it is even, and its digits still add to 18.
The trap is swapping the 2 with some other digit, or leaving it where it is. Then the number still ends in an odd digit, and 6 can never divide an odd number.
Remember: divisible by 6 means divisible by 2 and by 3. Check the digit sum for 3, and the last digit for 2.
A four-digit number: 9, star, 8, star. Both stars are the same digit, and 9 divides the number exactly. Which digit is the star?

spec.note: Both stars are the same digit.

beats.say: The test for 9: add up all the digits. If the total is in the 9 times table, then 9 divides the number.
The digits we know are 9 and 8. They add up to 17.
The two stars are the same digit. So together they add up to double that digit, and a double is always an even number.
The total must land in the 9 times table: 18, 27 or 36. For that, the stars must add 1, 10 or 19. Which of those can two equal digits make?

ask.ifNot: Two equal digits always add up to an even number. 1 and 19 are odd, so it must be 10.

beats.say: The two stars add up to 10, and half of 10 is 5. So each star is 5.
Let's check. The digits add up to 27, which is in the 9 times table. And the number is 9,585, which is 9 times 1065.
One trap: adding 1 just once would reach the 9 times table. But the star is there twice, so whatever we add is added twice.
In how many ways can 136 be written as one number times another? Each way is a pair of factors of 136.

spec.note: How many pairs multiply to 136?

beats.say: Start small. 1 times 136 is the first way. 136 is even, and half of it is 68. So 2 times 68 is the second way.
Try 3. The digits of 136 add up to 10, which is not in the 3 times table. So 3 does not divide it.
Try 4. For 4, look at the last two digits: 36. Does 4 divide 36?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 9 is 36. So 4 divides 136 as well.

beats.say: 4 times 34 is 136. Then 5, 6 and 7 do not divide 136. But 8 does: 8 times 17 is 136.
After 8, the next factor is 17, and that is already on the board as a partner. Going on would only repeat the pairs backwards.
So there are 4 ways.
Two traps. 17 times 8 is the same way as 8 times 17, so do not count it twice. And do not leave out 1 times 136.
Ajay writes the multiples of 4 up to 100. Vijay writes the multiples of 5 up to 100. How many numbers are in both notebooks?

board.text: Multiples of 4 and of 5, up to 100. In both = ?

beats.say: A number in both notebooks is a multiple of 4 and of 5. Count up in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20. The first one that 4 divides is 20.
So the numbers in both notebooks go up in steps of what?

ask.ifNot: Every number in both tables is a multiple of 20, the lowest common multiple. So they go up in steps of 20.

beats.say: That is 5 numbers. Or work it out: 100 divided by 20 is 5.
Two traps. 10 is in Vijay's notebook but not in Ajay's, so do not count in tens. And 20 is the smallest common number, not how many there are.
So for numbers in two tables at once: find the L C M, and count its multiples.
Find the H C F of 39 and 65. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 39 and 65 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 39?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 39, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 39: 1 times 39 and 3 times 13. So the factors of 39 are 1, 3, 13 and 39.
Do the same for 65. The pairs are 1 times 65 and 5 times 13. That gives the factors of 65: 1, 5, 13 and 65.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 13. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 13. Careful: 39 is in its own list, but it does not divide 65, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 13, so the H C F is 13.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 39 divided by 13 is 3, and 65 divided by 13 is 5. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
What is the 8th multiple of 9? The multiples of 9 are the numbers in the 9 times table.
The 1st multiple is 9 times 1. The 2nd is 9 times 2. The 3rd is 9 times 3. See the pattern?
So which sum gives the 8th multiple of 9?

ask.ifNot: The 1st multiple is 9 times 1, and the 2nd is 9 times 2. So the 8th multiple is 9 times 8.

beats.say: 9 times 8 is 72. So the 8th multiple of 9 is 72.
Check by counting up in 9s, eight times: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72.
Watch the neighbours. 81 is 9 times 9, the 9th multiple. And 63 is 9 times 7, the 7th multiple.
So the multiple number tells you what to multiply by. Easy!
How many factors does 12 have? A factor of 12 is a number that divides 12 exactly, with nothing left over.
Here is a neat trick. Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 12. The first pair is easy: 1 times 12.
Next we try 2. 12 is even, so 2 is a factor. What is its partner?

ask.ifNot: The partner is the number we multiply 2 by to make 12. Half of 12 is 6, so the partner of 2 is 6.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12. That is our second pair.
Keep going in order. The next number that works is 3: 3 times 4 is 12.
When do we stop? The next factor after 3 is 4, and 4 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 3 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 3 pairs. So we double 3.

beats.say: 3 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 6. So 12 has 6 factors. Here they all are, in order.
Remember the plan: go up in order, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and write each pair that works. Then count the numbers in the pairs.
Which of these is a prime number? A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. So we look for factors, and cross out any number that has more.
35 and 15 both end in 5, so 5 divides them. 35 is 5 times 7, and 15 is 3 times 5. Neither is prime.
Now 21. Is 21 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 7 is 21. So 21 has factors other than 1 and itself.

beats.say: 21 is 3 times 7, so it is not prime either.
That leaves 29. It is odd. Its digits add up to 11, so 3 does not divide it. It does not end in 0 or 5. And 7 times 4 is 28, which just misses it.
Nothing divides 29 except 1 and 29. So 29 is the prime number.
So to test for a prime, try the small primes 2, 3, 5 and 7. If none of them goes in, a number this size is prime.
Which of these four numbers can be divided exactly by 3? There is a quick test, so we will not need long division.
The test for 3: add up the digits. If the total is in the 3 times table, then 3 divides the number.
5,123 gives 11. 4,532 gives 14. 8,206 gives 16. None of those totals is in the 3 times table.
Now 7,251. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 7, then 2, then 5, then 1. You reach 15.

beats.say: The digits add up to 15, and 15 divided by 3 is 5, with nothing left over. So 7,251 is divisible by 3.
Let's check that the test told the truth. 3 times 2,417 is 7,251. It did!
So for 3, never mind how big the number is. Just add its digits and test the total.
Which of these four numbers can be divided exactly by 4? Again there is a quick test.
The test for 4: look only at the last two digits. If they make a number in the 4 times table, then 4 divides the whole number.

board.text: Test for 4: look at the last two digits

beats.say: 7,531 is odd, so it is out at once. 5,634 ends in 34. But 4 times 8 is 32 and 4 times 9 is 36, so 4 skips 34.
3,718 ends in 18. 4 times 4 is 16 and 4 times 5 is 20, so 4 skips 18 as well.
That leaves 2,316. Its last two digits make 16. Is 16 in the 4 times table?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 4 is 16. So the last two digits pass the test.

beats.say: 16 divided by 4 is 4, with nothing left over. So 2,316 is divisible by 4.
Here is the trap. 5,634 and 3,718 are even, but being even is not enough for 4. Always test the last two digits.
We need the H C F of 12 and 18. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both, with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 12?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 12, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 12: 1 times 12, 2 times 6 and 3 times 4. So the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Do the same for 18. The pairs are 1 times 18, 2 times 9 and 3 times 6. That gives the factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1, 2, 3 and 6. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 6. Careful: 12 is in its own list, but it does not divide 18, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 6, so the H C F is 6.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 12 divided by 6 is 2, and 18 divided by 6 is 3. Nothing is left over either time.
That is the whole method. Write both lists of factors, look for the numbers in both, and the biggest of those is the H C F.
We need the L C M of 6 and 8. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 6 times table and in the 8 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 8?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 8 is 8 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 8, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: The simplest way is to count up in both tables until they meet. Count up in 6s: 6, 12, 18, 24.
Now count up in 8s: 8, 16, 24.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 6 and 8?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 24 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 24 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 24.
Let's check. 24 divided by 6 is 4, and 24 divided by 8 is 3. Both divide exactly, so 24 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 6 by 8 gives 48. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 24 gets there first.
So for an L C M: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the answer. Your turn next!
We must write 60 as a product of prime numbers only. That is called its prime factorization.
Start with the smallest prime, 2. 60 is even, and 60 is 2 times 30.
30 is not prime, so we split it again. 30 is 2 times what?

ask.ifNot: Half of 30 is 15. So 30 is 2 times 15.

beats.say: 30 is 2 times 15. And 15 is not prime either: it is 3 times 5.
Now every piece is prime: 2, 2, 3 and 5. So 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Watch the traps. 2 times 3 times 10 does make 60, and so does 4 times 15. But 10, 4 and 15 are not prime.
So keep splitting until every number is prime. If any piece can still be split, you are not finished.
If a number can be divided by 6, which two numbers must also divide it, every time?

board.text: A number divisible by 6 must be divisible by ... ?

beats.say: Start with 6 itself. Which two numbers, other than 1 and 6, multiply to make 6?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 3 is 6. The other pairs multiply to make numbers bigger than 6.

beats.say: 6 is 2 times 3. So every multiple of 6 is built from a 2 and a 3. That means 2 divides it, and 3 divides it.
Let's test with 18, which is 6 times 3. 18 divided by 2 is 9. 18 divided by 3 is 6. Both are exact.
Why not 4? Try 6 itself. 4 goes into 6 once, with 2 left over. So 4 does not always work.
So a number divisible by 6 must be divisible by 2 and 3.
This works backwards too. To test for 6, test for 2 and for 3. If both pass, 6 divides the number.
Which pair of numbers is co-prime? Two numbers are co-prime when the only factor they share is 1.
So we look for a shared factor in each pair. If we find one bigger than 1, that pair is out.
8 and 12 are both even, and 4 divides both of them. 15 and 35 both end in 5, so 5 divides both. Those two pairs are out.
Now 6 and 9. Which number divides both of them?

ask.ifNot: 6 is 3 times 2, and 9 is 3 times 3. So 3 divides both.

beats.say: 6 and 9 share 3, so they are out as well.
That leaves 9 and 16. The factors of 9 are 1, 3 and 9. The factors of 16 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. The only number in both lists is 1.
Notice something. Neither 9 nor 16 is a prime number. Co-prime is about the pair: it means they share nothing but 1.
Is 4,518 divisible by 9? We can find out without dividing.
The test for 9: add up the digits. If the total is in the 9 times table, then 9 divides the number.
So add the digits of 4,518. What is 4 plus 5 plus 1 plus 8?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 4, then 5, then 1, then 8. You reach 18.

beats.say: The digit sum is 18.
And 18 is 9 times 2, so it is in the 9 times table. Yes, 4,518 is divisible by 9.
Let's check that the test told the truth. 9 times 502 is 4,518. It did!
One thing to notice. The digit sum does not have to be 9 itself. Any number in the 9 times table will do, and 18 is one.
What is the smallest composite number? A composite number has more than two factors.
We want the smallest, so start from the bottom and count factors. 1 has just one factor. It is not prime, and it is not composite.
2 has two factors, 1 and 2. 3 has two factors, 1 and 3. Exactly two factors means they are prime, not composite.
Now 4. How many factors does 4 have?

ask.ifNot: 1 times 4 is 4, and 2 times 2 is 4. So the factors are 1, 2 and 4. That is 3 factors.

beats.say: 4 has three factors: 1, 2 and 4. That is more than two, so 4 is composite. And it is the first one we met.
9 is composite too, because 3 times 3 is 9. But it is not the smallest.
So the order at the start is: 1 is neither, 2 and 3 are prime, and 4 is the smallest composite number.
Is 8,294 divisible by 11? There is a neat test for 11 that uses the digits.
Here is the test. Add the 1st and 3rd digits. Then add the 2nd and 4th digits. If the two sums are equal, or differ by 11, then 11 divides the number.

board.text: Test for 11: two sums equal, or differ by 11

beats.say: The 1st and 3rd digits are 8 and 9. They add up to 17.
The 2nd and 4th digits are 2 and 4. They add up to 6.
How far apart are the two sums, 17 and 6?

ask.ifNot: Take the smaller sum from the bigger one. 17 take away 6 is 11.

beats.say: 17 minus 6 is 11. The sums differ by exactly 11, so yes, 8,294 is divisible by 11.
Let's check that the test told the truth. 11 times 754 is 8,294. It did!
So for 11: add every other digit, and compare the two sums. Equal, or 11 apart, means yes.
One bell rings every 12 minutes, and another every 18 minutes. They ring together at 9 o'clock. When do they next ring together?

board.text: Bells ring every 12 and 18 minutes. Together at 9:00.

beats.say: Each bell rings at the multiples of its own number. They ring together at a common multiple, and the next time is the lowest one: the L C M.
The first bell rings after 12, 24, 36 and 48 minutes. The second rings after 18, 36 and 54 minutes.
What is the first number in both lists?

ask.ifNot: Run a finger along both lists. 36 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: 36 is the first number in both lists. So the L C M is 36, and the bells ring together after 36 minutes.
36 minutes after 9 o'clock is 36 minutes past 9.
Two traps. At 18 minutes past, only the second bell rings. And 30 is 12 plus 18, but it is in neither table, so no bell rings then.
48 apples and 36 oranges go into boxes. Every box holds the same number of fruits, all of one kind. What is the most each box can hold?

board.text: 48 apples, 36 oranges. Same number in each box.

spec.note: Same number in every box, as many as possible.

beats.say: The number in a box must divide 48 exactly, and 36 exactly. We want the biggest such number. What is that?

ask.ifNot: A number that divides both exactly is a common factor. The biggest one is the highest common factor.

beats.say: So we want the H C F. Here are the factors of 36. We test them on 48, starting from the big end.
36 does not divide 48. 18 does not: 18 times 2 is 36 and 18 times 3 is 54, so it skips 48.
Next is 12. Does 12 divide 48 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 4 is 48. So 12 divides 48 exactly.

beats.say: 48 divided by 12 is 4, and 36 divided by 12 is 3. So each box holds 12 fruits: 4 boxes of apples, and 3 boxes of oranges.
Watch the traps. 24 divides 48, but it does not divide 36. And 6 and 4 divide both, but they are not the biggest.
Which of these is a pair of twin primes? Twin primes are two prime numbers that are exactly 2 apart, like 3 and 5.
Every number in these pairs is prime. So the only thing to test is the gap. Subtract the smaller from the bigger.
17 minus 13 is 4. 7 minus 3 is 4. 13 minus 7 is 6. None of those gaps is 2.
Now the pair 11 and 13. What is the gap between them?

ask.ifNot: Count on from 11 to 13. That is 2 steps.

beats.say: 13 minus 11 is 2. Both are prime, and they are 2 apart. So 11 and 13 are twin primes.
The trap is thinking any two primes are twins. They must be exactly 2 apart, with just one number between them.
Which of these four numbers can be divided exactly by 8? There is a test for 8 too.
The test for 8: look only at the last three digits. If 8 divides the number they make, then 8 divides the whole number.

board.text: Test for 8: look at the last three digits

beats.say: 3,214 ends in 214. 8 times 26 is 208, so 6 is left over. 7,234 ends in 234. 8 times 29 is 232, so 2 is left over.
9,342 ends in 342. 8 times 42 is 336, so 6 is left over. That one is out as well.
Now 5,648, which ends in 648. 8 times 80 is 640, and that leaves 8. Does 8 go into what is left exactly?

ask.ifNot: 8 times 1 is 8. So after 640 there is exactly one more 8, with nothing left over.

beats.say: 80 eights and 1 more eight make 81 eights. So 648 divided by 8 is 81, and 5,648 is divisible by 8.
So for 8, cover up everything except the last three digits, and divide just those.
A number has exactly 2 factors. What kind of number must it be?

board.text: A number has exactly 2 factors. It must be ... ?

beats.say: Every number bigger than 1 has at least two factors: 1, and the number itself. Exactly 2 factors means nothing else divides it.
Take 5. Only 1 times 5 makes it. So its factors are just 1 and 5.
What do we call a number whose only factors are 1 and itself?

ask.ifNot: A number with only 1 and itself as factors is called a prime number.

beats.say: It is called a prime number. So a number with exactly 2 factors must be prime.
Look at the other choices. A composite number has more than 2 factors: 6 has four. The number 1 has only one factor. And an even number like 4 has three.
So remember: exactly two factors, 1 and itself, is what prime means.
6 is called a perfect number. Why? The secret is in its factors.

board.text: Why is 6 called a perfect number?

beats.say: List the factors of 6. 1 times 6, and 2 times 3. So the factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Now leave out 6 itself. The factors that are left are 1, 2 and 3.
Add up the factors that are left. What is 1 plus 2 plus 3?

ask.ifNot: 1 plus 2 is 3. And 3 plus 3 more is 6.

beats.say: 1 plus 2 plus 3 is 6. The smaller factors add up to the number itself! That is what makes 6 a perfect number.
It is not about having four factors. 8 has four factors as well, but 1 plus 2 plus 4 is only 7, not 8. So 8 is not perfect.
So a perfect number equals the sum of its factors, leaving out the number itself. They are very rare!
How can we tell that 5 divides a number, just by looking at its last digit?

board.text: Divisible by 5: the last digit is ... ?

beats.say: Let's look at the 5 times table itself: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
Read only the last digit of each number. What pattern do you see?

ask.ifNot: Read just the last digit of each number in the list: 5, 0, 5, 0, 5, 0.

beats.say: The last digits go 5, 0, 5, 0, again and again. They are never anything else.
So a number is divisible by 5 when its last digit is 0 or 5.
Watch the traps. Saying 0 only would miss 15 and 25. Saying 5 only would miss 10 and 20. We need both.
And an even last digit is not the rule. 8 is even, but 5 does not divide 8.
We need the first three common multiples of 4 and 6: the first three numbers that are in both times tables.

board.text: First three common multiples of 4 and 6 = ?

beats.say: Now count up in 6s: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36.
What is the first number that is in both lists?

ask.ifNot: 6 is not in the 4 times table. 12 is the first number that is in both lists.

beats.say: 12 is in both. Keep looking along the lists: 24 is in both, and so is 36. Ring them.
So the first three common multiples are 12, 24 and 36. Did you notice? They are the 12 times table.
One trap: 18 is in the 6 times table, but not in the 4 times table. A common multiple must be in both.
Two mystery numbers. Their H C F is 6 and their L C M is 36. One of the numbers is 12. We must find the other.

board.text: HCF = 6, LCM = 36. One number is 12. Other = ?

beats.say: Here is a handy fact. For any two numbers, the H C F times the L C M equals the two numbers multiplied together.

board.text: HCF × LCM = one number × other number

beats.say: So 6 times 36 is the same as 12 times the other number. And 6 times 36 is 216.
So 216 is 12 times the other number. How do we find the other number?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 12, we divide by 12.

beats.say: 216 divided by 12. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 8 is 96. Together that is 216, so the answer is 18.
Let's check. 12 times 18 is 216 as well. And 6 goes into 18 exactly 3 times, just as an H C F should.
So remember: H C F times L C M gives the product of the two numbers. Divide by the number you know, and the other one appears.
Which of these four numbers can be divided exactly by 10?
Think of the 10 times table: 10, 20, 30, 40. Every number in it ends in 0. That is the whole test.
7,105 ends in 5. 8,901 ends in 1. 4,055 ends in 5. None of them ends in 0, so they are out.
Which number ends in 0?

ask.ifNot: Look only at the very last digit. 3,200 is the one that ends in 0.

beats.say: 3,200 ends in 0, so it is divisible by 10. In fact 3,200 divided by 10 is 320.
Here is the trap. The other three numbers have a 0 in the middle. That does not count. Only the last digit matters.
How many prime numbers are there between 10 and 20? Let's write out the numbers in between, and cross out the ones that are not prime.

board.text: How many primes are there between 10 and 20?

beats.say: The even numbers can all be divided by 2, so they are not prime. Cross out 12, 14, 16 and 18.
The odd ones are left: 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19. Which of these is not prime?

ask.ifNot: 15 ends in 5, so 5 divides it. 3 times 5 is 15.

beats.say: 15 is 3 times 5, so it is not prime. Cross it out.
11, 13, 17 and 19 are left. None of them is in the 3 times table, and none ends in 5. They are all prime.
Count them: 11, 13, 17, 19. There are 4 prime numbers between 10 and 20.
The trap is 15. It is odd, so it can look prime. Always test odd numbers for 3 and for 5.
There is only one even number that is prime. Which one is it?
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. So let's count the factors of the even numbers.
Start with 2. Only 1 times 2 makes it. Its factors are 1 and 2. Exactly two, so 2 is prime.
Now 4. What are the factors of 4?

ask.ifNot: 1 times 4 is 4, and 2 times 2 is 4. So the factors are 1, 2 and 4.

beats.say: 4 has three factors, which is too many for a prime. 6 has four: 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Here is why. Every even number bigger than 2 can be divided by 2, as well as by 1 and itself. That is at least three factors. So 2 is the only even prime.
And 0 is not a prime number at all. The primes start from 2.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes is a way of sifting numbers. Up to 50, we cross out the multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7. What kind of numbers are left?

board.text: Sieve up to 50: cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7.
What kind of numbers are left?

beats.say: In the sieve, 1 is crossed out at the very start. We keep 2, 3, 5 and 7 themselves, and cross out all their other multiples.
A composite number is made by multiplying smaller numbers. Up to 50, one of those smaller numbers must be 2, 3, 5 or 7.
Why? 7 times 7 is 49, nearly 50. The next prime is 11, and 11 times 11 is 121, far past 50. So nothing up to 50 can be built from bigger primes alone.
So does every composite number up to 50 get crossed out?

ask.ifNot: Every composite number up to 50 has 2, 3, 5 or 7 as a factor. So it is a multiple of one of them, and it gets crossed out.

beats.say: Every composite number is gone. The numbers left have no smaller factor at all. Here are the ones after 7.
A number with no factor except 1 and itself is prime. So the numbers left in the sieve are prime numbers.
They are not all multiples of 11, because 13 and 17 are there too. And they are not even: the even numbers went first.
Five numbers: 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71. One of them does not belong with the others. Which one?
They all end in 1, and they go up in tens. So the pattern is not the clue. Think instead about what kind of numbers they are. 31 and 41 are prime.
Let's test 51 for 3, by adding its digits. 5 plus 1 is 6. Is 6 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 2 is 6. So the digit sum is in the 3 times table, and that means 3 divides 51.

beats.say: So 3 divides 51. In fact 51 is 3 times 17. It is not prime!
Now the others. Their digits add up to 4, 5, 7 and 8. None of those is in the 3 times table. They are odd, they do not end in 5, and 7 skips them all. They are prime.
Four primes, and one number that is not. So 51 does not belong.
The trap is that 51 looks prime. It is odd and it ends in 1. But adding the digits shows that 3 divides it.
We need the L C M of 15 and 9. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 15 times table and in the 9 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 15?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 15 is 15 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 15, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Let's write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 15s: 15, 30, 45.
Now count up in 9s: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 15 and 9?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 45 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: 45 is in both lists, and nothing before it is. So the L C M is 45.
Let's check. 45 divided by 15 is 3, and 45 divided by 9 is 5. Both divide exactly, so 45 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 15 by 9 gives 135. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 45 gets there first.
That is the idea of an L C M: the first meeting point of the two tables. Write out the multiples and look for the first match.
We need the L C M of 9 and 3. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 9 times table and in the 3 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 9?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 9 is 9 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 9, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Look closely at these two numbers. 9 is in the 3 times table: 3 times 3 is 9.
So where do the two tables first meet?

ask.ifNot: 9 is the very first number in its own table, and we just saw it is in the 3 times table too. So the two tables first meet at 9.

beats.say: Here are both tables. 9 is in each of them. Nothing smaller can be, because 9 is where its own table starts. So the L C M is 9.
One trap to watch for: do not just multiply them. 3 times 9 is 27. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one.
Remember this one. If the bigger number is already in the smaller number's table, the bigger number is the L C M.
Find the L C M of 12 and 10. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The simplest way is to count up in both tables until they meet. Count up in 12s: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 12 and 10?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 60 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 60 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 60.

Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 12?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 12 is 12 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 12, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Look closely at these two numbers. 12 is in the 6 times table: 6 times 2 is 12.
So where do the two tables first meet?

ask.ifNot: 12 is the very first number in its own table, and we just saw it is in the 6 times table too. So the two tables first meet at 12.

beats.say: Here are both tables. 12 is in each of them. Nothing smaller can be, because 12 is where its own table starts. So the L C M is 12.

Find the H C F of 72 and 60. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 72 and 60 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 72. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, then 3, and 3 is left. So 72 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 3.
Take 60. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, then 3, and 5 is left. So 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 72 and 60 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have two 2s and a 3. Careful: 72 has three 2s, but 60 has only two 2s. So only two 2s are shared.
The middle of the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 2 times 3 is 12. So the H C F is 12.

spec.note: The middle holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 72 divided by 12 is 6, and 60 divided by 12 is 5, with nothing left over. And 6 and 5 share no factor except 1, so nothing bigger works.
So the plan for an H C F of bigger numbers: break both into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!

We need the H C F of 65 and 91. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both, with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 65?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 65, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 65: 1 times 65 and 5 times 13. So the factors of 65 are 1, 5, 13 and 65.
Do the same for 91. The pairs are 1 times 91 and 7 times 13. That gives the factors of 91: 1, 7, 13 and 91.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 13. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 13. Careful: 65 is in its own list, but it does not divide 91, so it is out.
The picture shows it too: the shared factors sit in the middle. So the H C F of 65 and 91 is 13.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 65 divided by 13 is 5, and 91 divided by 13 is 7. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 6 and 4. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 6 and 4 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 4?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 4, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We write down all the factors of each number. Then we pick the biggest one they share.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 6: 1 times 6 and 2 times 3. So the factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6.
Now 4. Its pairs are 1 times 4 and 2 times 2. So the factors of 4 are 1, 2 and 4.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 2. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 2. Careful: 4 is in its own list, but it does not divide 6, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 2, so the H C F is 2.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 4 divided by 2 is 2. Nothing is left over either time.
That is the whole method. Write both lists of factors, look for the numbers in both, and the biggest of those is the H C F.

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: Counting up in 9s would take a long time. Here is a quicker way: count up in the bigger number, 16, and test each one.
Which is the first number in the list that 9 divides exactly?

ask.ifNot: Try dividing each one by 9. It only goes in exactly when we reach 144.

beats.say: 9 does not go exactly into 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 or 128. But 9 times 16 is 144. So the L C M is 144.
Let's check. 144 divided by 16 is 9, and 144 divided by 9 is 16. Both divide exactly.
Did you notice? The L C M is just 16 times 9. That happens when the two numbers share no factor except 1.
So here is a quick way to an L C M: count up in the bigger number, and stop at the first one the smaller number divides.

In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 4, so the H C F is 4.

Find the H C F of 24 and 60. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

60 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 24 divided by 12 is 2, and 60 divided by 12 is 5. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 5 have nothing more in common.
